readerTitle: The cook who saw the mistake and said nothing
caseNote: 가상 사례 (호텔 주방, 가사 청소 업체) + 실제 관찰 (주방의 브리게이드 체계와 'Heard, chef' 같은 콜백 관행)
insight: 실수가 새는 곳은 대개 '모두의 일'로 남은 인수인계와, 본 사람이 말하지 못하는 순간이다. 이름 붙은 담당자와 말해도 안전한 분위기는 함께 있어야 작동한다.
misconception: 사고가 나면 실수한 사람을 찾아 엄하게 책임을 묻는 것이 재발을 막는 가장 확실한 방법이다.

sources.text: Edmondson, A. (1999). Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams. Administrative Science Quarterly, 44(2).
전문 주방의 브리게이드 체계 (일반적으로 19세기 말 Auguste Escoffier가 정리한 것으로 알려짐)
주방 사례와 청소 업체 사례는 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: 브리게이드 체계를 Escoffier가 정리했다는 설명은 널리 알려진 내용이지만, 카드에는 'usually credited to'로 완화해 적었습니다. 게시 전 요리사 교육 자료로 확인하세요.
'Heard, chef', 'Behind' 같은 콜백은 영미권 주방에서 흔히 쓰이는 관행으로 관찰된 내용입니다. 특정 주방의 규칙으로 일반화하지 않았습니다.
소프트웨어 장애 대응의 '단일 책임자(incident commander)'와 '비난 없는 회고(blameless postmortem)'는 업계에서 널리 쓰이는 관행으로, 특정 기업 수치는 인용하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The cook who saw the mistake and said nothing
body: Friday night in a busy hotel kitchen. A ticket reads *nut allergy*. The plate goes out with a pesto that contains pine nuts.
A server catches it at the table, just in time. Later, a junior cook admits she noticed the ticket. She didn't say anything. Everyone assumed someone else had checked.

image.label: Busy hotel kitchen pass with one cook hesitating
image.brief: 따뜻한 일러스트. 분주한 호텔 주방의 패스(음식 내보내는 선반). 요리사들이 빠르게 움직이는데, 앞치마를 맨 젊은 요리사 한 명만 주문표를 보며 멈칫하고 입을 다문 모습. 실제 호텔 로고나 브랜드 없음.

cards.title: You're the head chef. What do you do first?
body: No guest was hurt, but it was close. Your kitchen sits inside a large hotel, and the hotel manager wants to know what you'll change.
Which move comes first?

options.text: Find out who plated the dish and give them a written warning
options.feedback: It shows you take it seriously, but it teaches the team that mistakes get punished. That hurts **psychological safety**: next time, people hide what they see.

options.text: Name one person to check every allergy ticket at the pass, and ask the junior cook what stopped her speaking up
options.feedback: This fixes both leaks. **Roles and accountability** gives the check an owner. Asking without blame builds **psychological safety**, so the next warning gets said out loud.

options.text: Hold a team meeting to remind everyone how serious allergies are
options.feedback: Good intent, but nothing changes. The check still belongs to everyone, which means no one, and the junior cook still doesn't know if speaking up is welcome.

cards.title: A good kitchen runs on owners and call-backs.
body: Professional kitchens often use the **brigade system**, usually credited to the French chef Auguste Escoffier. Every station has one owner: sauces, grill, fish, pastry. Nobody wonders whose job the sauce is.
Kitchens also use call-backs. When the chef calls an order, cooks answer "Heard, chef." When someone walks past with a hot pan, they say "Behind." Saying it out loud is part of the job.
The pesto slipped through a gap in both habits.

cards.eyebrow: Concept at work · Roles and accountability
cards.title: "Everyone checks allergies" means no one does.
body: Every station had an owner. The allergy check didn't. It sat between the cook, the person plating and the server, so each assumed another had done it.
**Roles and accountability** means each task, especially each handoff, has one named owner. Others can help. One person answers for it.
The fix is small: one person at the pass reads every allergy ticket before a plate leaves.

image.label: Kitchen stations, each with one owner, and a gap at the pass
image.brief: 주방 평면도 인포그래픽. 'Sauce', 'Grill', 'Fish', 'Pastry' 스테이션마다 요리사 아이콘 한 명씩. 가운데 'Allergy check' 칸만 물음표로 비어 있다가, 오른쪽 그림에서는 이름표가 붙은 한 사람이 채운 모습.

cards.softwareNote: Software teams handle outages the same way. One named incident lead runs the response, and the review afterward looks for what broke in the process, not who to blame.

cards.title: She saw it. The kitchen made it hard to say.
body: Kitchens are loud, fast and ranked. The newest cook has the least status. Stopping a plate means questioning someone senior in front of everyone.
**Psychological safety** is a shared belief that you won't be punished or mocked for speaking up. Without it, the person closest to a problem stays quiet.
A head chef can build it on purpose: thank the person who stops a plate, even when they turn out to be wrong. One public thank-you teaches more than a speech.

cards.title: A cook flags the fish. The sous chef snaps.
body: Two weeks later, during the rush, a cook says the fish smells off. Your sous chef, your second in command, snaps: "Not now. Plate it." The cook goes quiet.
After service, what do you do?

options.text: Back your sous chef. Speed matters in a rush
options.feedback: You protect the sous chef's authority, but every cook learns that food-safety warnings are unwelcome. That undoes the **psychological safety** you just started building.

options.text: Talk privately with the sous chef: food-safety flags always get a ten-second check, and the sous chef makes the call
options.feedback: The sous chef keeps authority without public embarrassment. **Roles** stay clear about who decides, and **psychological safety** stays real because flags always get heard.

options.text: Tell the cook to bring concerns straight to you next time
options.feedback: The cook feels heard, but you skip the sous chef and blur **roles**. You also become a bottleneck on every busy night.

cards.title: Safe isn't soft, and clear isn't rigid.
body: Psychological safety doesn't mean lower standards. The best kitchens are demanding *and* safe: the bar stays high, and admitting a miss is how you meet it.
Clear roles have a trap too. Pushed too far, they become "not my station." Owning a task doesn't stop you from helping a neighbor who's drowning in tickets.
One owner, many helpers, and anyone allowed to say stop.

cards.title: Now it's a home cleaning crew.
body: You run a cleaning company. Three-person crews clean homes. A client complains that a spare bedroom was skipped. Each cleaner thought another had done it. The newest one noticed the closed door but didn't ask.
What do you change?

options.text: Dock a little pay from all three cleaners
options.feedback: Shared blame feels fair but owns nothing. It also teaches crews to hide misses, the opposite of **psychological safety**.

options.text: Split rooms by name before each job, and end with a two-minute walk-through where anyone can flag a miss
options.feedback: Named rooms give each task an owner (**roles and accountability**). The walk-through gives the newest cleaner a normal moment to speak up (**psychological safety**).

options.text: Have the crew lead personally inspect every room
options.feedback: Now one person owns quality, but jobs run longer and the others stop checking their own work. The newest cleaner still has no easy way to speak up.

cards.softwareNote: The same fix works for a product team before a release: each checklist item has a named owner, and a short final review where the newest engineer can say "wait."

cards.title: Give every handoff an owner, and make it safe to say stop.
body: You used two ideas from this unit: **roles and accountability**, so every task and handoff has one named owner, and **psychological safety**, so the person who sees a problem says it out loud. Either alone leaves a gap.
**Try it today:** pick one handoff in your team. Can you name who owns it? Then ask your newest person what they noticed last week but didn't mention.
